title: Hunger and thirst ask for a place (1.2)
word: Hunger and thirst ask for a place
hook: once the gods have moved in, two more voices speak up: hunger and thirst want a home too
tomorrow: the self enters through the crown of the head

segments.voice: Yesterday: the person, the house the gods called well made. Your line was the gods within. Did you speak today as if there were fire in your mouth? Day four hundred one.

Everyone's moved in. Fire has the mouth, the sun has the eyes, the moon has the heart. The house is full and humming. And then there's a knock. Two figures are standing outside, and they've been there since before the gods arrived. In fact, they're the reason the gods went house-hunting at all. Their names are hunger and thirst. And they say to the self: what about us? Find us a place too. These two are easy to recognize. They turn up mid-afternoon, at midnight in front of the fridge, in long meetings. The Aitareya gives them a whole verse.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS FULL.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `HUNGER AND THIRST: WHAT ABOUT US?`

segments.voice: Here's the order in the story. Back when the gods first fell into the great ocean, the self touched that whole creation with hunger and thirst. That's why the gods asked for a home: they wanted a place to eat. So hunger and thirst are older than the house. They didn't break in. They were part of the plan. Now, with the gods settled, the two of them ask: find a place for us. And the self doesn't banish them. It doesn't scold them as enemies of the spirit. It says, more or less: I'll give you a share among these gods. You'll be partners with them. And the text explains what that means. That's why, whenever an offering is made to any god, hunger and thirst share in it. It's an ordinary arrangement, and a generous one. One way to hear it: when your eyes see, they get hungry for more seeing. When your ears hear a song, they want the next one. When the mind, the moon in the heart, settles on an idea, it gets thirsty for another. On this reading, every power comes with an appetite. The story doesn't call that a flaw. It gives hunger and thirst a home, right alongside fire and sun. Some later teachers read this passage as a sober account of the human condition: wanting runs through every sense. But the story itself is calm about it. In the story, nobody is shamed for being hungry. The self knows who lives in the house, and gives each one its share.
screen: `HUNGER AND THIRST WERE THERE FIRST.` · `THEY ASK: FIND US A PLACE.` · `A SHARE IN EVERY GOD'S OFFERING.` · `EVERY POWER COMES WITH AN APPETITE.` · then, large: `THEY TOO NEED A HOME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your appetites. Sit, and check: is there hunger, even a little? Thirst? Some other wanting, for your phone, for news, for this to be over? Whatever's there, don't obey it and don't fight it. Just find where it lives in the body. The stomach. The throat. The hands. Let it have that small place, the way the story does. Notice that it can sit there, known and given room, without running the house. The bell holds the time.
Hunger and thirst ask for a place. In the Aitareya, they're given no room of their own, but a share in whatever is offered to every god.
Your line: they too need a home. Today, when a craving shows up, instead of scolding it, name it and give it a seat: you're hunger, I know you. Day four hundred one.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Aitareya read this passage when explaining why appetite goes with every sense, and in Vedic ritual each offering is made to a particular deity, the share the passage says hunger and thirst join.

original.note: Sanskrit aśanāyā-pipāse: hunger (aśanāyā) and thirst (pipāsā), a pair in Aitareya 1.2.

trapdoor: what you thought: hunger is the enemy of the spiritual life.
what it means: in the Aitareya, hunger and thirst are older than the gods' home, and are given a share in every god.
what a scholar hears: tasmād yasyai kasyai ca devatāyai havir gṛhyate, bhāginyāv evāsyām aśanāyāpipāse bhavataḥ: whatever god receives an offering, hunger and thirst become sharers in it (1.2.5).
